segs.text: Module seven A, objective one. Drug product performance, bioavailability and bioequivalence. Drug product performance is the release of the drug substance from the drug product, the step that leads to its bioavailability. It comes first because drug that stays in the tablet is never absorbed. She said, If the drug does not release from dosage form, then the drug will not be available for the body to use.

card.m: drug product performance: release of the drug substance from the product
release → absorption → systemic circulation
no release: no drug available

segs.text: Bioavailability is the rate and extent to which the active ingredient is absorbed from a product and becomes available at the site of action. Extent is how much of the dose gets into the systemic circulation, and rate is how fast. Extent is read from the area under the plasma level against time curve, A U C, a concentration times a time. The area is proportional to the amount of unchanged drug that reaches the circulation, so in the same person more drug in gives more area. F, the fraction of the dose that reaches the circulation, is the extent half; it has no units and is one for an I V dose.

card.m: bioavailability = rate and extent of absorption
extent: how much gets in. rate: how fast
extent: AUC, in (mg/L)hr
same patient: more drug in → larger AUC
F = fraction reaching the circulation, no units; F<sub>IV</sub> = 1

segs.text: Rate is read from t max, the time of the peak. At first absorption brings drug in faster than elimination removes it, so the level rises. At the peak the two rates are equal, so faster absorption gets there sooner, at a smaller t max. More drug absorbed at the same speed gives a larger area, the same t max. t max equals the natural log of k a over k, divided by k a minus k, with k a and k the absorption and elimination rate constants: no F, no dose. A U C equals F times the dose, D zero, over k times the volume of distribution, V D, with F on top and no k a, so changing k a alone moves the peak, not the area.

card.m: rate: t<sub>max</sub>, in hr
at t<sub>max</sub>: rate of absorption = rate of elimination
faster absorption → smaller t<sub>max</sub>
more absorbed, same speed: AUC larger, t<sub>max</sub> unchanged
t<sub>max</sub> = {{frac:ln(k<sub>a</sub>/k)|k<sub>a</sub> − k}}: no F, no dose
AUC = {{frac:F D<sub>0</sub>|k V<sub>D</sub>}}: F on top, no k<sub>a</sub> → k<sub>a</sub> alone moves t<sub>max</sub>, not AUC

segs.text: Bioequivalence compares the same active ingredient in two products, a test product and the reference, the standard or originator it is compared with. They are bioequivalent when there is no significant difference in the rate and extent of availability at the site of action, at the same molar dose under similar conditions. Since bioavailability has two parts, both must match: the area and the peak time. She said, It's the absence of a significant difference. So they don't have to be exactly the same, but they just can't be too different.

card.m: test against reference: same active ingredient
no significant difference in rate and extent
same molar dose, similar conditions
bioequivalent: AUC similar and t<sub>max</sub> similar
similar, not identical

segs.text: Her bioequivalence example puts three formulations of one drug, A, B and C, on one plot. A and B enclose the same area, so the same amount got in, but B peaks later, so it got in more slowly. A and C peak at the same time, but C encloses half the area, so C delivered half as much drug at the same speed. So A and B differ in rate, A and C in extent, and no pair is bioequivalent. A fourth curve she drew close to A, with about the same peak time and area, is the one she called bioequivalent.

card.m: A, B: AUC<sub>A</sub> = AUC<sub>B</sub>; B peaks later
A, C: same t<sub>max</sub>; AUC<sub>C</sub> = ½ AUC<sub>A</sub>
none of A, B and C is bioequivalent to another
D: close to A in AUC and t<sub>max</sub> ✓

segs.text: In her items, the rate and extent of absorption from one product is bioavailability, a comparison of two products is bioequivalence, and the release step is drug product performance. Two products with similar F values are not shown to be bioequivalent, because F and A U C give extent only. She said, these two have similar F's, but you don't know if they're bioequivalent because you don't know about the, the rate. A bioequivalence study is a specialized relative bioavailability study, the comparison of objective two, that compares rate as well as extent.

card.m: one product: bioavailability. two products: bioequivalence. release: product performance
similar F: extent only, rate unknown → bioequivalence not shown
bioequivalence study: relative bioavailability study + rate
